scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that leans toward principle while granting that compromise is sometimes needed; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Leaders are pulled between standing firm on principle and bending to public demands.
Some believe effective leaders must yield to public opinion and abandon principle for compromise, while others believe the key quality is staying committed to principles.
I lean toward the value of principle, but I believe some willingness to compromise is also necessary.
First, staying committed to principles is essential to truly effective leadership.
A principled leader gives her people direction and something to believe in.
For example, great reformers changed the world by refusing to abandon their core beliefs.
This shows that steady principle can achieve what constant compromise never could.
Leaders who abandon every principle for popularity soon stand for nothing at all.
People also lose respect for a leader who changes her values with every shift in opinion.
For these reasons, commitment to principle is a vital quality.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why compromise is also needed

sentences.text: Second, however, some willingness to compromise is also necessary in real leadership.
In a divided society, refusing ever to bend can lead only to conflict and deadlock.
Consider a leader who must compromise on small points to pass a law that helps millions.
Such compromise shows wisdom, not weakness, when it serves a greater good.
A leader who ignores public opinion entirely may lose the support she needs to govern.
Listening to the people and adjusting where wise is part of leading well.
Effective leaders, then, hold to principle while compromising on lesser matters.
In conclusion, commitment to principle is at the heart of effective leadership.
But a willingness to compromise on smaller matters is also necessary to get things done.
The best leaders stay true to their principles while bending wisely where compromise serves the greater good.
